extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of the history of American journalism; journalism students and historians
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative principles and standards embedded in a historical textbook account of 19th-century American newspapers (Bennett, Greeley, the Herald and the Tribune). Useful for analysing editorial practice, press influence, and historiographic judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive news-getting and exclusive reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The editor/journalist should actively gather and generate news: 'did all his own reporting, collected all his own news, wrote the entire paper himself.' The capacity to produce exclusive material (scoops) is a mark of journalistic distinction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in text: Bennett's hands-on reporting and the Bennetts' reputation for revolutionizing 'news-getting' and for 'exclusive news.' Practical effect: exclusive or novel accounts (e.g., Bennett printing his own assault account) raised circulation. Anti-pattern: relying solely on others' dispatches or republishing without original reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational or personal incidents to attract readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing vivid, personal, or sensational accounts (even of the editor's own experiences) to draw public attention and increase circulation: e.g., Bennett printed an account of his assault and circulation rose to 9,000 copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text presents this as an innovation and a commercial success (circulation boost). It also notes the social reaction (elite 'horrified' vs. mass appeal). Scoring note: effective for reach but ethically debatable; consider trade-off between popularity and decorum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to mass audience versus elite respectability
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper can be judged by whether it appeals to broad working-class readership through lively, dynamic writing rather than the 'respectable' but sleepy tone of conservative dailies: penny press style aimed at readers the conservative sheets would 'have sent... to sleep.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage contrasts Bennett's dynamic outbursts (which attracted laborers and draymen) with conservative six-cent papers. Use as a criterion to evaluate editorial style and market positioning: accessibility, energy, and mass-market resonance score highly here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial courage and refusal to be intimidated
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor's integrity includes willingness to 'tell the honest truth' despite threats, assaults, or attempts at intimidation: Bennett's proclamations that 'neither Webb nor any other man shall or can intimidate me.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measured by continued publication of contentious material, open denunciation of opponents, and personal perseverance. Caveat: courage must be balanced with accuracy and responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy maintained despite sensational tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational or populist treatment of news does not excuse factual inaccuracy; contemporary critics and later observers noted that even sensational papers (e.g., the Herald for 1858-59) could be 'accurate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villard's observation is cited: although Bennett was seen as a sensationalist/blackguard, certain Herald issues treated news 'in a manner very mild compared to ... conservative dailies' and were accurate. Guidance: evaluate both tone and factual reliability separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence balanced with principled advocacy
rubrics_metrics.description: A desirable editorial posture is 'removed alike from servile partisanship on the one hand and from gagged, mincing neutrality on the other' — i.e., openly advocate guiding principles yet be ready to expose and condemn unworthy conduct even in one's own party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted from Greeley: a paper should 'advocate the principles and commend the measures of that party to which his convictions allied him, yet frankly dissent from its course on a particular question.' Use this as a standard for editorial independence and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial openness to reformist and minority ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: A newspaper's quality can be measured by its willingness to provide columns to reform movements and minority viewpoints (e.g., Greeley opened his columns to Fourierists, socialists, and advocates of women's emancipation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Alfred Brisbane's Fourier articles; Margaret Fuller's contributions. Guidance: diversity of viewpoints and engagement with reform causes indicate editorial breadth and public-service orientation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility via price and distribution to reach laboring classes
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper aimed at the laboring classes should be cheap and broadly distributed (the 'cheap daily' or penny press model) to engage readers unable to afford higher-priced papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greeley's stated motive: a cheap daily 'addressed more especially to the laboring class' was needed. Practical metric: price point, street distribution (newsboys), and circulation among working-class neighborhoods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of newspapers as instruments of political influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are to be judged by their capacity to shape public opinion and political outcomes — the text traces a progression from early critics of government to Greeley, who became 'the most influential single figure in the selection of the country's presidents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess editorial reach, influence on party politics (e.g., Free Soil, Republican), and active campaigning. Ethical note: influence entails responsibility to truth; evaluate both power and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid presentism in historiographic judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: When studying the history of journalism, 'seeing the past in the light of present-day developments... must be studiously avoided' — historians should not judge 19th-century practices by modern moral standards without context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for historical evaluation: consider contemporary social norms, audience composition, and technological/economic constraints. Anti-pattern: anachronistic condemnation that ignores historical circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal characteristics relevant only when they affect public mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The personal character of an editor is 'not of vital importance, unless those personal characteristics are obtruded in such a way as to corrupt the public mind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personal biography as explanatory only when it materially shaped editorial policy or public discourse (e.g., partisan bias, moral corruption affecting reporting). Avoid overemphasizing private morality when it had no public consequence.
